source_excerpt: Der hatt. W. heißt Taru (syll. dTa-a-ru, dDa-a-ru, van Gessel, HittPantheon 1, 449-451, gelegentlich auch dŠa-a-ru, s. ibid. 376; logogr. dIŠKUR bzw. d10); der Name des auch theriomorph als Stiergott* (vgl. auch W.* C. § 1) dargestellten Taru ist vielleicht mit dem in sem. und indogerm. Sprachen bezeugten Stierwort zu verbinden (Wettergottgestalten 126 Anm. 871). ... Es ist auffällig, dass es sich beim Namen des heth.-luw. W. um ein Appellativ handelt, das keine Entsprechung in anderen indogerm. Panthea hat und lautlich an hatt. Taru anklingt. Es handelt sich daher wahrscheinlich um eine in Anlehnung an hatt. Taru geformte Neubildung (Oettinger 2006, 474). Der heth.-luw. Tarḫu(nta) wäre dann nichts anderes als der von Luwiern und Hethitern adaptierte altanatol.-hatt. W.- und Stiergott.

fresh_retrievals.locator: Lead paragraph; infobox 'Language family' field; 'Classification' section; 'Corpus' section
quoted_passages: Hattic, or Hattian, was a non-Indo-European agglutinative language spoken by the Hattians in Asia Minor in the 2nd millennium BC. Scholars call the language "Hattic" to distinguish it from Hittite, the Indo-European language of the Hittite Empire.
Language family: Unclassified language isolate

Certain similarities between Hattic and both Abkhazo-Adyghean and Kartvelian languages have led to proposals by some scholars about the possibility of a linguistic bloc from central Anatolia to the Caucasus.
According to Alexey Kassian, there are also possible lexical correspondences between Hattic and Yeniseian languages, as well as with the Burushaski language

No document has been found in which native Hattic-speakers wrote their own language. Scholars must rely on indirect sources or mentions by their neighbours and successors, the Hittites. Some Hattic words can be found in religious tablets of Hittite priests that date from the 14th and the 13th centuries BC. The passages contained, between the lines of the text signs, the explanation "the priest is now speaking in Hattic".
Documents from Hattusa span CTH 725–745. Of these CTH 728, 729, 731, 733, and 736 are Hattic/Hittite bilinguals.
fresh_retrievals.passage_support_scope: Hattic is non-Indo-European and is not Hittite; Hattic survives inside Hittite ritual tablets (CTH 725–745, bilinguals 728/729/731/733/736) with an explicit 'speaking in Hattic' cue; Caucasian/Yeniseian/Burushaski links exist as scholarly proposals, not as a demonstrated relation.
fresh_retrievals.limits: Tertiary source; the article self-labels parts of the conquest narrative and some classification statements as needing citations; the 'isolate' label is a database convention, not proof that no relation exists. No Hattic text read directly (none survives in native transmission per this source).

quoted_passages: In Hattian (a non-Indo-European language), he was called Taru; in Luwian, Tarḫunz (Cuneiform: Tarḫu(wa)nt(a)-, Hieroglyphic: DEUS TONITRUS); in Palaic, Zaparwa; in Lycian, Trqqas/Trqqiz; and in Carian, Trquδe (dat.).

Norbert Oettinger has argued that the functions of the Anatolian weather god ultimately come from the Proto-Indo-European god Perkwunos, but that they did not preserve the old name to coin instead the new epithet Tṛḫu-ent- ("conquering"), which sounded close to the name of the Hattian Storm-god Taru.

quoted_passages: Der hatt. W. heißt Taru (syll. dTa-a-ru, dDa-a-ru, van Gessel, HittPantheon 1, 449−451, gelegentlich auch dŠa-a-ru, s. ibid. 376; logogr. dIŠKUR bzw. d10); der Name des auch theriomorph als Stiergott* (vgl. auch W.* C. § 1) dargestellten Taru ist vielleicht mit dem in sem. und indogerm. Sprachen bezeugten Stierwort zu verbinden (Wettergottgestalten 126 Anm. 871).

Der Name des heth.-luw. W. ist in verschiedenen Formen bezeugt, die alle auf die indogerm. Wurzel *terh₂w- zurückgehen, die auch in heth. tarḫu- „mächtig sein“ fortgesetzt ist (Starke 1990, 136−145; Hawkins 2005, 295; Kloekhorst 2006, 98f.).

Die wichtigste luw. Form des Namens ist die Partizipialbildung Tarḫwant-, Tarḫunt- (keil.-luw. Tarḫunz sekundär auf -a thematisiert ...

Es ist auffällig, dass es sich beim Namen des heth.-luw. W. um ein Appellativ handelt, das keine Entsprechung in anderen indogerm. Panthea hat und lautlich an hatt. Taru anklingt. Es handelt sich daher wahrscheinlich um eine in Anlehnung an hatt. Taru geformte Neubildung (Oettinger 2006, 474). Der heth.-luw. Tarḫu(nta) wäre dann nichts anderes als der von Luwiern und Hethitern adaptierte altanatol.-hatt. W.- und Stiergott.

Raw unnormalized extraction available at the recorded txt path, lines 7774–7836.
fresh_retrievals.passage_support_scope: Scholarly reference-work passage: the Hattic storm-god is named Taru (with syllabic spellings dTa-a-ru/dDa-a-ru); the Hittite-Luwian name continues IE *terh₂w- (tarḫu- 'be mighty'); the key Luwian form is Tarḫunt-/Tarḫwant- and Hittite forms a-stem Tarḫunta-; the Anatolian name is judged 'probably' a new formation modelled on Hattic Taru, i.e. contact-adaptation rather than one unchanged original god. This directly upgrades the round-6 evidence from authored teaching to a signed reference-work article.
fresh_retrievals.limits: Reference-work summary, not the primary monographs: it cites, among others, 'Klinger J. 1996: Untersuchungen zur Rekonstruktion der hattischen Kultschicht (= StBoT 37)' — the exact round-6 named monograph — and van Gessel's HittPantheon, which remain unread directly. No cuneiform autograph read. The adaptation judgment is presented as probable ('wahrscheinlich'), not certain.

quoted_passages: The two varieties of Luwian are known after the scripts in which they were written: Cuneiform Luwian (CLuwian) and Hieroglyphic Luwian (HLuwian). There is no consensus as to whether these were a single language or two closely related languages.
It was once thought to be a variety of the Hittite language, and the term "Hieroglyphic Hittite" was formerly used to refer to the language of the same inscriptions, but this term is now obsolete.

The absence of the syllabic symbols from the seals makes it impossible to determine the pronunciation of names and titles that appear on them, or even to make a certain attribution of the text to a specific language.

In the 1970s, as a result of a fundamental revision of the readings of a large number of hieroglyphs by John David Hawkins, Anna Morpurgo Davies, and Günter Neumann, it became clear that both cuneiform and hieroglyphic texts recorded the same Luwian language.
fresh_retrievals.passage_support_scope: Script names corpora, not ethnicities or dialects: the two Luwian varieties are named after their scripts; script attribution does not settle language (logogram-only seals cannot even fix the language of a name/title); the older 'Hieroglyphic Hittite' label is obsolete. Directly supports entry lines 61, 69 and 74.
fresh_retrievals.limits: Tertiary; the one-vs-two-languages question is itself flagged as unsettled on this page.

quoted_passages: The dominant inhabitants in central Anatolia at the time were the Hatti (from whom the word "Hittite" was later derived). There were also Assyrian colonies in the country; it was from these that the Hittites adopted cuneiform script.
In this time frame, Hittite and Luvian and Palaic were the "big three" Anatolian languages, all being recorded in cuneiform inscriptions.
fresh_retrievals.passage_support_scope: Political/ethnic label 'Hatti' and the language label 'Hittite' are distinguished; the cuneiform script was adopted from Assyrian merchant colonies (script adoption is not language identity); one script serves multiple languages.
